summary: A practical guide for administrators who need to protect the computers and networks of a site connected to the Internet. It covers writing security policies, a range of technical security topics, and how to respond when an incident happens. It is informational and replaces RFC 1244.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a how-to book for the people who look after a school's or company's computers, explaining how to lock the doors and what to do if someone breaks in.

subtitle: A practical guide for site administrators on writing security policy, protecting systems and responding to incidents.

tldr.problem: Sites connected to the Internet need to decide what to protect, from what, and how to react when security fails, but have no shared framework for doing so.
tldr.mechanism: The handbook walks administrators through risk assessment and security policy, the architecture of services and firewalls, security services such as authentication and auditing, and a staged approach to handling incidents.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational framework, not a standard. It replaces RFC 1244 and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

today: RFC 2196 is an informational document that obsoletes RFC 1244. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose, Audience and Risk Assessment
sections.content:
The handbook is a guide to setting computer security policies and procedures for sites that have systems on the Internet. It is written for system and network administrators and for decision makers, typically middle management. It is not aimed at programmers writing secure programs. It describes itself as only a framework: a site still has to make decisions, gain agreement, and then communicate and implement its policies.

The basic approach has five steps: identify what you are protecting, determine what you are protecting it from, determine how likely the threats are, implement cost-effective measures, and review continuously. One old truism it repeats is that the cost of protecting against a threat should be less than the cost of recovering if the threat struck.

Risk assessment starts by listing assets (hardware, software, data, people, documentation and supplies) and threats. The classic threats it names are unauthorized access, disclosure of information, and denial of service. For each asset the goals are availability, confidentiality and integrity.
sections.plainLanguage: Before locking up your treasures, you first list what you own and who might try to take it. Then you spend your effort where it matters most.

sections.title: Security Policies
sections.content:
A security policy is defined as a formal statement of the rules that people given access to an organization's technology and information assets must follow. Its goals come from three trade-offs: services offered versus security, ease of use versus security, and cost of security versus risk of loss.

The handbook lists who should help write the policy, from the site security administrator and technical staff to user representatives, management and legal counsel. A good policy must be implementable, enforceable with tools or sanctions, and clear about who is responsible for what. Its components include purchasing guidelines, and privacy, access, accountability and authentication policies, plus an availability statement, a maintenance policy, a violations reporting policy and supporting information.

Once established, the policy should be communicated, and staff should sign that they have read and agreed to it. It should be reviewed regularly and kept flexible, largely independent of specific hardware and software, with exceptions spelled out.
sections.plainLanguage: A security policy is the rulebook for a clubhouse. Everyone helps write it, everyone reads it, and it gets updated when things change.

sections.title: Architecture, Services and Firewalls
sections.content:
The architecture chapter says every site should have a comprehensive security plan that sits above individual policies. It contrasts two philosophies. In a deny all model, all services are turned off and enabled case by case. This is generally more secure but takes more work. In an allow all model, everything is on by default and holes are patched as found. The text warns against a hard outer shell with a soft middle: once the firewall is breached, subverting the internal network is trivial.

Other advice: separate services onto different hosts, keep internal and external services apart, and evaluate new services skeptically. The handbook then covers protecting the infrastructure and network (including protecting routing updates with passwords, checksums or encryption) and services such as DNS, mail, the Web, FTP and TFTP, and NFS. For example, it says TFTP should be avoided as much as possible, and that the security server itself should not be reachable from off-site.

A firewall is described as one of several mechanisms to control and watch access to and from a network, usually built from filtering routers and proxy servers. The text stresses that firewalls are not a cure-all and are only one part of the solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a castle with one gate guarded by sentries, and with the kitchen, the armory and the guest rooms in different buildings so trouble in one does not spread.

sections.title: Security Services and Procedures
sections.content:
This chapter introduces the services a site may need. For authentication, it recommends moving away from standard reusable passwords because they often cross networks in clear text and are captured by packet sniffers. It points to one-time passwords and Kerberos, and gives advice on choosing and protecting secrets and on password assurance: robust passwords, changing default passwords, shadow passwords, password aging, account blocking and the finger daemon.

It also covers confidentiality (encryption), integrity (cryptographic checksums such as MD5 rather than the UNIX sum program), authorization (owner, group and world permissions, and access control lists), and access: physical access, walk-up network connections, other network technologies and modems.

Auditing advice includes collecting login and access-change events and a timestamp, never gathering passwords (including incorrect ones), and weighing three storage methods: a read/write file, a write-once device, or a line printer. Backups should be made, kept off-site, verified, and not assumed to be good.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the everyday habits: use a different secret each time, check that nothing was quietly changed, write down who came in, and keep a spare copy of your work somewhere safe.

sections.title: Handling Security Incidents
sections.content:
The incident chapter says the operative philosophy is to react according to a plan, since decisions made in haste can damage tracking down the source, collecting evidence and recovering. Planning includes dry runs and defined goals. It suggests five priorities: protect human life and safety first, then classified or sensitive data, then other data, then prevent damage to systems, and finally minimize disruption of computing resources.

It stresses establishing points of contact in advance, including a single coordinator, and deciding what is shared with users, the public and other sites. Identifying an incident means checking whether it is real, taking a system snapshot early and starting a log book. The handling steps are notification, protecting evidence, containment, eradication, recovery and follow-up, ending in a postmortem and a written report. Afterward the site should take inventory, revise its plan and redo its risk analysis.

Responsibilities include not crossing the line by using non-public facilities of remote sites to chase intruders, and good Internet citizenship by alerting other sites that may be affected.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong, you follow a fire drill you practiced: stay calm, stop it spreading, clean up, get back to normal, and then talk about how to do better next time.

sections.title: Ongoing Work and Resources
sections.content:
The handbook says security is never finished. Its starter list of ongoing activities includes subscribing to advisories from incident response teams such as the CERT Coordination Center, installing vendor patches, watching configurations for changes, reviewing policies and procedures at least annually, reading relevant mailing lists, and having compliance checked by someone other than those who wrote the policies.

The final chapters list publicly available tools and mailing lists and give a long bibliography. The text itself warns that many of the listed tools will be surpassed or made obsolete.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping a house safe is a chore you repeat: check the locks, fix the broken ones, and keep learning about new tricks burglars use.

items.label: Human life and safety
items.desc: Always takes precedence over everything else.

items.label: Classified or sensitive data
items.desc: Prevent exploitation and inform affected sites.

items.desc: Proprietary, scientific, managerial and other data.

items.desc: Loss or alteration of system files, damage to disk drives.

items.desc: Of computing resources, weighing shutdown against staying up.
